A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multilingual political-bias study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison, including image-based material. Many translated statements, prompts, and examples are retained despite renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original Political Compass Test evaluations of 13 LLMs and framing, entity, and sentiment analyses of generated headlines, with additional results in the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds deterministic-decoding comparisons, uncertainty summaries, and further framing and error analyses.

M1.justification: The core PCT/framing pipeline and stance-score functions remain. However, v2 describes task-specific mDeBERTa fine-tuning in Appendix B.4 and zero-shot classification in B.5; B.7 also conflicts with the retained Urdu fine-tuning account in Section 5.1. Actual training changes cannot reliably be distinguished from inconsistent new documentation.

E1.justification: The five Pakistani languages, 62 PCT statements, and 11 headline topics are retained. English already appears in v1's cross-language findings in Section 5.4; v2 supplies explicit numerical comparisons. Added decoding and uncertainty analyses do not introduce distinct language or task coverage.

E2.justification: The principal 13-model PCT and four-model headline comparisons are retained. Appendix B.4 newly reports pilot comparisons of mDeBERTa against XLM-R and mBERT, absent from v1, although quantitative pilot results and protocols are not supplied.

E3.justification: V1 specifies temperature 0.5 throughout. V2 adds deterministic temperature-0.0 evaluation while retaining 0.5, including the four-model comparison in Figure 5 and Table 5. It also introduces confidence-weighted error metrics in Table 3, substantially extending the evaluation design without establishing that every original experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds deterministic-decoding robustness evidence, error analyses across frame categories and languages, a confidence-related analysis, and broader comparisons of framing distributions across topics and stances. These additions extend v1's selected framing examples and DeepSeek analysis. The quantity analyzed in Figure 15 is inconsistently described.

E5.justification: Beyond the retained Fleiss' kappa reporting, v2 introduces bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals, bootstrap errors, confidence summaries, and confidence-weighted errors in Figure 10 and Table 3. Figure 10 states n = 10, but the resampling and repeated-generation procedures remain insufficiently specified; an increase in independent runs is not established.

E6.justification: V2 adds deterministic PCT scores, bootstrap metrics, and aggregate polarity/polarization results; Figure 19 reports polarization of 0.630 for Gemini and 0.510 for GPT-4. It also changes the Balochi positions in Figure 4 relative to v1 Figure 2, conflicting with its own Table 4. The added decoding results use different experimental conditions.

T1.justification: The stance-scoring and discretization functions, neutrality-distance definitions, and Fleiss' kappa formula are retained. V2 adds standard ratio and probability formulas explaining existing frame-frequency, entity-frequency, and sentiment calculations, without new theoretical results, proofs, or substantive mathematical revisions.

C1.justification: The central contributions and language-dependent bias claims remain. The novelty claim is narrowed from v1's first comprehensive investigation within a multilingual, non-Western framework in Section 2 to a first framework/evaluation specifically for Pakistani languages in v2 Sections 1–2.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning missing cultural counterfactuals, prompt effects, classifier bias, architectural differences, translation procedures, and single-response variability. Appendices C.8–C.9 introduce interpretations about model family and size not guaranteeing neutrality. New accounts of fine-tuning effects and confidence-related findings also introduce interpretive inconsistencies.

D1.justification: The new technical appendix documents model identifiers and architectures, classifier inputs and label selection, Selenium-based PCT submission, and prompting procedures. V2 also discloses a 150-token maximum and translation-consensus procedures. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although conflicting classifier and fine-tuning descriptions remain.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused discussion of Pakistani-language NLP, citing Urdu QA, NER augmentation, and Urdu benchmarking work. It also adds Röttger et al.'s PCT critique and stance-detection references while removing some general citations. The central positioning around multilingual political bias and framing remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial portions of the results prose are rewritten. V1 Sections 5.3–5.5 are reworked into a separate Findings section, and the appendices are reorganized around expanded Technical Details and Detailed Results sections.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the framework, compass, and entity diagrams; combines four headline-validation heatmaps into Figure 3; and relocates several main-text displays to the appendices. It adds numerous diagnostic plots and numerical tables, changes appendix layout, and revises labels, captions, and image borders.

improvement.justification: Tables 2–5 and Appendix B make previously mostly plotted results and loosely specified procedures more inspectable. However, v2 introduces consequential inconsistencies: Figure 4 places GPT-4-turbo's Balochi result in the lower-left quadrant despite Table 4 reporting (2.88, 0.97), and Appendix C.4 and Figure 15 disagree over whether the plotted quantity is framing intensity or bootstrap error. Conflicting fine-tuning accounts further limit reproducibility. These documentation gains and problems in the new evidence prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
